If there's a unity, it has to be the kind that survives real diversity, the way a symphony holds a cello and a trumpet. And the claim comes from inside the text. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus, "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets... interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27).

Jesus's first preaching was about the kingdom, which we've shrunk into heaven, a cause, or a feeling. The word means reign: God stepping in to be king of his world again, arriving like a seed rather than an army. And we live in the overlap, the already and the not yet. The kingdom has truly come and hasn't yet come in full, which is why faith can feel like winning and losing in the same hour.

keyScripture.why: "And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). The claim that the whole Bible is one story bending toward a person comes from inside the text, on the lips of its central figure.

discussion.q: How have you usually read the Bible, as a set of separate lessons and verses, or as one story? What changes if it's one story moving toward one person?
discussion.behind: Bring the usual way of reading into the open. Many of us treat the Bible as a shelf of lessons and end up with a verse on a mug and no sense of where we are in the story. The aim is to feel the difference between mining for application and finding your place in a story already underway, where he is the center and we aren't.

discussion.q: Read Luke 24:13-32. The two disciples had the right books and couldn't see the person walking beside them. Where have you read the Old Testament for rules, or for yourself, and missed who it was pointing toward?
discussion.behind: The problem on the road wasn't a worse library but a different way of seeing. Help the room recognize the habit of reading Scripture for principles and proof texts while missing the Christ it reaches for. Then notice verse 32: "Did not our hearts burn within us?"

discussion.q: When you hear "the kingdom of God," what comes to mind first, heaven after death, a better society, or an inner peace? What does the full idea of God's reign ask that the smaller version doesn't?
discussion.behind: Each of the three contains a fragment and none is the whole. Help people find which one they live by: the escape, the project, or the private peace. The real kingdom puts God on the throne, which unsettles all three.

discussion.q: Read Mark 4:26-32. Jesus says the kingdom grows like a seed, slowly and out of sight. Where have you lost heart because God's work didn't come with the power or speed you expected?
discussion.behind: Make room for honest disappointment. John the Baptist expected an axe and fire and got a teacher healing lepers while he sat in prison (Matthew 11:2-6). Let people name where they've lost heart because the kingdom didn't come on their schedule.

discussion.q: Read Romans 8:18-25. Where do you feel the tension between what God has already done in you and what isn't finished yet? Have you blamed the Bible for promising too much, or yourself for believing too little?
discussion.behind: Close on the overlap, and turn it inward. Leaders often perform the "already" while privately living in the "not yet," and the performance sends struggling people home to fight alone. Offer the third option: the fight is evidence that the new has begun. Go first.

objections.objection: The Bible is obviously an anthology, sixty-six books written over a thousand years by dozens of authors, assembled by committees long after the fact. Any unity people find in it was read in later by believers who needed it to hang together.
objections.response: That deserves its full weight, because on the surface it's largely true. The Bible wasn't handed down whole from the sky. It was gathered, the Christian canon recognized at councils late in the fourth century, and the differences inside it are real. Job argues with the easy answers and God sides with him. Ecclesiastes refuses cheerful conclusions. The four Gospels don't tell the resurrection morning in the same order. So any unity can't be the unity of a memo where every voice says the same thing, and flattening the Bible into one bland message erases it. But the unity it has is the kind that survives real diversity, the way a symphony holds a cello and a trumpet. And the claim doesn't come from later interpreters tidying up. It comes from inside the text, from the risen Christ on the Emmaus road, and from Jesus's own words: "it is they that bear witness about me" (John 5:39). You find that unity by following the story the books tell, not by forcing it on from outside.

objections.objection: The "already and not yet" idea is theology covering its failures. Whatever the gospel promised and didn't deliver gets filed under "not yet," and whatever it did produce gets filed under "already." The scheme can never be wrong because it can never be checked.
objections.response: That's a fair charge, and it would be serious if the idea had been invented afterward to explain disappointment. But it's there from the start. Paul doesn't fall back on it when his churches let him down; he builds his picture of the present on it. "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). That's the already, without a hedge. And the same Paul writes that "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now... and we ourselves... groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:22-23). That's the not yet, just as plain. Oscar Cullmann compared it to a war in which the decisive battle is won long before the fighting ends. The cross and resurrection were the decisive day; the renewal of all things is the final day. We live in the costly interval. Far from a dodge, it fits the actual texture of Christian life.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where do you most feel the war between the new life that has really begun and the old self that hasn't finished dying? Have you been hiding it because you thought a real Christian should be done fighting?
sessions.practice: This week, change how you read and how you measure. When you open the Bible, don't go looking for a nugget to apply to your day. Read one passage as a chapter in a single story moving toward Christ, and ask where it sits in that story and where you sit, a late chapter and not the center. And when you feel the familiar discouragement of an old sin or a fresh loss, don't file it as failure. Name it as the overlap, the new pressing into the old, and let the groan be the groan of childbirth and not of a funeral. Write down what shifts when you stop blaming the book and stop blaming yourself.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, the whole story was bending toward your Son all along, and we kept reading the right books with the wrong eyes, mining for our own principles and missing the one standing in front of us. Forgive us for shrinking your kingdom to fit our preferences, an escape when we wanted comfort and a project when we wanted to feel important, anything that kept us on the throne instead of you. We live in the overlap, and it's hard. We've blamed your book and blamed ourselves and hidden the fight from one another. Teach us to groan in hope, the groan of birth and not of death, toward the morning that is surely coming. The decisive day is behind us. Bring the final one. Amen.
reflection: Where have I read Scripture as a quarry for proof texts, and what would change if I read it as one story moving toward Christ, with me as a late chapter rather than the center?
Which small version of the kingdom have I settled for, the escape, the project, or the private feeling? What does God's full reign ask of me that the small version lets me avoid?
Where have I hidden the fight between the already and the not yet, performing a victory I didn't have? What would it cost to let others see that I'm still fighting?
sessions.teaching:
Open most Bibles and the table of contents tells you it's a collection. Sixty-six books, two testaments, written over more than a thousand years by farmers and kings and fishermen and a tax collector, in three languages. Every honest reader has to start where the skeptic starts. This looks like an anthology, a shelf rather than a story. The real question is whether the unity people claim to find is actually there, or whether it was read in later by people who needed it to hang together.

That objection deserves its full weight, because on the surface it's largely true. The Bible wasn't handed down whole from the sky. It was gathered, and the Christian canon wasn't formally recognized until councils late in the fourth century, Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397, confirming what the churches already used. Scholars like James Barr warned against forcing a false theological unity on books that were diverse and often in tension. And the differences are real. Job argues with the easy answers his friends keep offering, and God sides with the man who argued. Ecclesiastes refuses cheerful conclusions. The Gospels don't even tell the resurrection morning in the same order. So if there's a story holding these books together, it can't be the unity of a memo. It has to be the kind that survives real diversity, the way a symphony survives the difference between a cello and a trumpet.

I believe the books do hold together, and the center has a name. The claim doesn't come from later interpreters anxious to tidy things up. It comes from inside the text, from its central figure. On the road to Emmaus, after the resurrection, a stranger falls in with two grieving disciples, and "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). They had been reading the right books with the wrong eyes. Jesus said the same to the religious teachers of his day: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me" (John 5:39).

The story has a shape you can recognize. It opens with creation and a garden, a good world and a humanity made to bear God's image. It breaks almost at once, and the rest is the long account of God refusing to abandon what he made: calling Abraham, rescuing slaves from Egypt, giving a law, raising kings, sending prophets, until the prophets begin to speak of something new, a king who won't fail, a servant who will suffer, a covenant written on the heart. Then the Gospels open, and the story that had been straining for a thousand years arrives at a person: the true image-bearer, the faithful Israel who keeps the covenant the nation broke, the king from David's line, the suffering servant, the lamb the whole sacrificial system had been pointing to. Geerhardus Vos, who taught at Princeton and is often called the father of Reformed biblical theology, argued that revelation isn't a flat field of timeless statements but an unfolding history growing toward Christ.

When that person comes out of the wilderness in Mark, his first preaching isn't about love or grace in general. It's about the kingdom: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel" (Mark 1:15). We've spent a long time making that word smaller. Ask what the kingdom means and you'll usually hear one of three answers. Heaven, the place your soul goes after death. A better society, the cause you organize for. A feeling, an inner peace. Each holds a fragment, but none is the thing. The Greek word basileia, like the Hebrew behind it, means first of all reign, rule, not territory. George Eldon Ladd spent his career pressing that point. When Jesus says the kingdom is at hand, he isn't announcing an address for the afterlife. He's announcing that God is stepping in to be king of his world again. That's why he taught us to pray, "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10).

And it didn't look like an arrival. There was no army; Rome didn't fall. The reign of God came in a wandering teacher healing the sick, eating with the wrong people, forgiving sins, driving out evil. He said the kingdom was like a mustard seed, "the smallest of all the seeds on earth," that grows until "the birds of the air can make nests in its shade" (Mark 4:31-32), and like leaven working quietly through dough. It came like a seed in the soil, not an army at the gate. That's why John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was really the one. John had announced an axe at the root and fire, and the one he announced went around healing lepers and telling stories while the wicked stayed in power and John stayed in his cell. If John struggled, our confusion is in good company.

That leads to what may be the truest thing the New Testament teaches about the present. It's often called the already and the not yet, a phrase Ladd made familiar. The kingdom has truly arrived in Jesus, and it hasn't yet arrived in full, and the whole Christian life is lived in the overlap. You aren't crazy, and you aren't uniquely failing. The new creation has truly begun and the old order hasn't finished dying, both at once, in the same body, on the same ordinary Tuesday.

The skeptic's objection deserves a hearing: isn't "already and not yet" just a way of filing every failure under "not yet" so the faith can never be wrong? That would be serious if the idea had been invented afterward. But it's built in from the start. Paul writes, "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). That's the already, stated without a hedge. And the same Paul writes that "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now," and that "we ourselves... groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:22-23). That's the not yet, just as plain. Oscar Cullmann, writing just after the Second World War, compared it to a war in which the decisive battle is won long before the fighting ends: the outcome is settled, and soldiers still die for months afterward. The cross and resurrection were the decisive day. The renewal of all things is the final day. We live in the long, costly interval between.

This fits what Christian life actually feels like. Expect the already with no not yet, and every lingering sin and every new grave will crush you. Expect the not yet with no already, and your faith will be all waiting and no power. Holding both lets you breathe. The right response isn't triumph or despair. It's hope, not a vague wish but a settled confidence that because the decisive day has come, the final day surely will. You groan, because the grave is real and the old habit isn't dead yet, but you groan the way a woman groans in labor, because something is being born. The fight against the old self isn't evidence the gospel failed. It's evidence that two ages overlap in you, and the defeated one doesn't give up its ground quietly. That you're fighting at all shows the new has begun.

Many of us have read this book the wrong way for long stretches, hunting for sermon material or the verse that would win an argument, treating the story as a quarry and ourselves as the one with the pick. And pastors hide their own fight, standing in front of people performing the already while privately living deep in the not yet, fighting the same fears they fought ten years ago. I know that performance from the inside. It tells struggling people the war should already be over and sends them home to fight alone.

So when your faith feels like winning and losing in the same hour, stop choosing between blaming the book and blaming yourself. The two on the road were reading the right books with the wrong eyes, and the cure wasn't a better library. It was the risen Jesus explaining himself. The decisive day is behind you, the final day is ahead, and everything in between is meant to be carried in hope, toward a morning that is surely coming and isn't here yet.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at what's called biblical theology, the practice of following the single storyline of Scripture instead of mining it for separate lessons. Geerhardus Vos argued that revelation isn't a flat field of timeless statements all equally available at every point, but an unfolding history growing toward Christ. You don't read the Old Testament well by pretending it already knows everything the New Testament will say. You read it well by watching it lean forward, reaching for a fulfillment it senses but can't yet see. Set that against the proof-text habit that treats the Bible as a quarry of principles, and ask what that habit costs: the verse on the coffee mug cut loose from its story, the self at the center of a book that's finally about what God has done.

Then weigh the framework of the already and the not yet, which Ladd made familiar and Cullmann pictured as the decisive day and the final day of a war. The comfort is real: feeling victory and defeat at once isn't a malfunction, it's the normal shape of life in the overlap. So is the danger the skeptic names, that the idea can be misused as an excuse for everything that disappoints us. Faithful readers have to hold both truths without collapsing either: no triumphalism that expects the already with no not yet, and no resignation that expects the not yet with no already.

leaderPrimer:
A doctrine study tends to draw two kinds of people, and the danger they create together is worth seeing before the first week. The first comes with strong opinions about inerrancy and church history and little patience for slower company. The second sits down already sure the conversation will go over their head, because somewhere along the way the church taught them theology belongs to the confident. Left alone, the first will talk and the second will disappear into polite nodding, and you'll finish five weeks having run a seminar that formed no one. That's this room's particular hazard: doctrine handled as a trophy instead of as food.

Your job is traffic control in service of something deeper. Ask for stories before positions. The study rests on the claim that the gospel we announce and the creed we recite aren't academic furniture but news, the kind a man runs into the street to tell, and news belongs to everyone at the table equally. I came to these doctrines from atheism, which is one reason the study keeps translating instead of assuming. You can promise your nervous members that no prior vocabulary is required.

Watch session two closely. Arguments about the Bible are rarely only about the Bible; they're about fear. When someone gets loud about Scripture, hear the fear before you answer the claim. Session three, on sin and grace and the God who bled, is where the room will go quiet in a good way. Let it. Session four asks people to receive the church's long memory, including centuries some of them were taught to skip, and someone may bristle at how much weight the tradition gets. Take the bristle seriously and keep going. By session five the study wants every member to find their own small life inside the one story Scripture tells. That's the real test of your five weeks. Not whether anyone can define the hypostatic union on demand, but whether the woman who believed theology wasn't for her has started using it on an ordinary Tuesday without noticing. Aim everything at her.

faq.q: Is this study going to be over my head if I'm not a theologian?
faq.a: No. It's written for ordinary believers, skeptics, and anyone whose faith has outgrown the slogans they were handed, not for seminary. Every doctrine is tied to a concrete picture: the herald announcing the war is over, the father running down the road, the judge stepping down from the bench, the seed hidden in the soil. The scholars and councils are there to show the depth is real and was hard-won, not to make you feel small. Every discussion question carries a note for the leader, and the leader's guide warns against turning the room into a contest over who knows most.

faq.q: I have real doubts about whether any of this happened. Am I welcome here?
faq.a: You're the reader I most want to write for. The study doesn't flinch from the hardest version of the questions. It grants that the Bible looks like an anthology, that we have no original manuscripts, that the canon was recognized by councils in the fourth century, that the word "Trinity" isn't in the Bible and was argued out at councils emperors called, and that the most educated century was also among the bloodiest. It says what's true in each objection before answering. Paul stakes the gospel on whether one weekend happened and invites people to check. That isn't how someone talks who is afraid of your doubt. Bring your questions.

faq.q: Why does the study spend so much time on old councils and dead theologians instead of just the Bible?
faq.a: Because a church that doesn't know what was already settled is at the mercy of whoever is most confident in the room. The councils and creeds aren't rivals to the Bible. They're the church reading the Bible out loud together across centuries and writing down what it found, so the children wouldn't have to fight the same fights from scratch. Nearly every teaching the councils rejected was a way of making the faith easier to believe, and each, looked at closely, emptied the gospel. The study holds that no creed stands above Scripture, but reading Scripture with no memory is how Arius read it, sincerely and intelligently, and he arrived at a Christ who couldn't save.

faq.q: What does it mean to say the gospel is news and not advice?
faq.a: It means the gospel is first a report of something God has done in history, not a program for what you should do or a reassurance about how you already are. The word, euangelion, belonged to heralds announcing that a battle was won. The study takes seriously the two sincere ways we lose this: making the gospel the call to follow Jesus's example, which becomes a ladder no one can climb, or making it the assurance that God loves you as you are, which, if it's the whole message, means nothing actually happened. News is harder than advice, because advice you can adjust to taste and news changes the world whether you agree or not.

faq.q: How can the Trinity be practical? It sounds like math I'm supposed to affirm and forget.
faq.a: If God is, in his own eternal life, a communion of persons loving one another before there was a world, then love isn't something God picked up when he made creatures. It's what he is. A God who was one solitary person would have needed a world in order to love, and a God who needs you has to take from you what completes him. The triune God was already full and glad before the first star, so when he turns toward you he's overflowing, not filling a hole. He doesn't love you because he's lonely. That's the difference between a faith that wears you out, always paying a god who needs something, and one that holds you.

faq.q: Isn't the doctrine of sin just a dark, guilt-producing view of people?
faq.a: The study argues the opposite: it's the only account honest enough to hold our glory and our cruelty together, and it's good news the way a true diagnosis is good news to someone told for years nothing was wrong. The view that people are basically good struggles to explain why the most educated century was among the bloodiest, and it leaves you alone with your failures and no words for them. The Christian account says the worst thing about you is real, named, no surprise to God, and already carried, so you can stop pretending.

faq.q: Why insist that grace is costly? Isn't the whole point that grace is free?
faq.a: Both are true, and holding them together is the point. Grace is free to the one who receives it and costly to the one who gives it. The son walks into the feast for free, but the calf is dead. The study takes aim at what Bonhoeffer called cheap grace, grace we give ourselves, forgiveness without repentance, a warm mood that asks nothing and so changes nothing. Real grace humbles the legalist, who thinks it must be earned and so never rests, and the sentimentalist, who thinks it cost nothing and so uses it to excuse what should be put to death.

faq.q: What is the "already and not yet," and why does it matter to me?
faq.a: It may be the most pastorally important idea in the study. The kingdom of God has truly arrived in Jesus, and it hasn't yet arrived in full, and the Christian life is lived in the overlap. That's why faith can feel like victory and defeat at once. You really are a new creation, and the old self really is still dying, in the same body on the same ordinary Tuesday. Many believers swing between blaming the Bible for promising too much and blaming themselves for believing too little. Both are wrong. Oscar Cullmann compared it to a war whose decisive battle is won long before the fighting ends. That you're fighting at all shows the new has begun.

faq.q: Does the study claim the Bible has no errors at all, or does it allow for problems?
faq.a: It tries to step back from the usual way that argument is fought. Both a certain kind of believer and many skeptics assume that truth means precision by modern standards, so that a rounded number or a speech given in summary counts as failure. Careful defenders of inerrancy reject that assumption too. The study points to the claim Scripture makes for itself: the faithfulness of God, and a word given to make people "complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Christians who love the Bible use different words here, inerrant, infallible, trustworthy, and the study doesn't ask your group to settle which is best. It does ask that the gospel not be staked on whether an ancient book behaves like a modern almanac, and it treats the differences between the resurrection accounts as the mark of real witnesses.

faq.q: I'm a lifelong churchgoer who can recite all of this. Is there anything here for me?
faq.a: Yes, and you may need it most, because knowing the words well is exactly when they stop touching you. The study asks whether the love came first for you in practice or only on paper, whether you pray to the triune God or to a lonely idol you're always trying to satisfy, whether you confess justification by faith on Sunday and keep a ledger by Monday, whether you perform the already while hiding the not yet. I don't exempt myself from any of those questions, and the study asks the same of you. The point isn't new facts but letting the old depths you can already recite become ground you actually stand on.

faq.q: Why does the study keep turning the questions back on the writer and the leader?
faq.a: Because a teacher who points only at other people's errors lets the room stay comfortable and changes no one. Depth handed down from above gets received as either a burden or a boast. I don't teach these doctrines as someone who has them sorted. I've preached the ladder and called it grace, prayed to a lonely god while confessing the Trinity, and kept a ledger I say Christ has torn up. A teacher who can admit that can lead a room into the same truthfulness, which is where doctrine stops being information and becomes repentance. The study asks every leader to do the same.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm not sure I believe all of it myself?
faq.a: Your uncertainty isn't a disqualification, and pretended certainty would be worse. The study is meant to be led by a fellow traveler, not an expert handing out answers. Every discussion question carries a note for you, every objection is given its strongest form before it's answered, and every session ends in prayer, so you aren't improvising the hard parts. Being truthful about your own questions may be the most pastoral thing in the room. What you need is to take every objection seriously before answering, to keep the room safe for the doubter, the churchgoer and the skeptic alike, to refuse to use knowledge as a weapon, and to keep pointing everyone, yourself first, toward the God who needed nothing and came anyway.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. Going down to the roots of the faith means letting some things we've recited for years be asked about again. Three things before we start. First, this is a safe room for hard questions. You can say "I'm not sure I believe this." You can ask whether any of it happened. Nobody will be told to stop thinking or made to feel small for what they don't know. Second, when someone raises a hard objection, we'll try to find what's right in it before we answer it. Third, I'm in this too. I confess this faith with my mouth and deny it with my life more often than I'd like to admit. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone has to have an answer.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage and the doctrine actually say. Now let's bring it into the week we're about to walk into, where it either holds our weight or doesn't, because these old depths were never meant to be admired. They were meant to be stood on.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop here, even though some of it isn't tidy. The church kept the mystery and gave up the neatness on purpose, and pretending we've solved it all would be a lie. Take this toward God this week rather than carrying it as one more thing you're supposed to have figured out. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions. And if tonight raised a real question or a real failure, don't bury it; bring it back next time. Let me pray for us before we go. Thanks for being here.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and hard questions, and explain that objections will be heard at full strength before they're answered. Take session 1's opening questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, The News, and the God It Is About, part one: the gospel as news rather than advice, and the two sincere ways we lose it.
Week 3: Session 1 continued: the God the news is about, the Trinity, and the love that needed nothing, with the practice.
Week 4: Session 2, The Word You Can Trust: the fear underneath the arguments, faithfulness, and the manuscripts and the canon.
Week 5: Session 3, The Fracture, the Gift, and the God Who Bled, part one: sin as a true diagnosis and good news.
Week 6: Session 3 continued: costly grace, and why only one who was both God and man could reach across the gap, with the practice.
Week 7: Session 4, The Church Remembers: the councils and creeds as memory, and the question underneath the Reformation.
Week 8: Session 5, One Story, and the Overlap We Live In: the single story bending toward Christ, the kingdom, and the already and not yet, with a time of looking back at the end.

bibliography.title: The Doctrine of God (Reformed Dogmatics)
bibliography.author: Herman Bavinck
bibliography.note: Bavinck's treatment of God as complete in himself and of the Trinity. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: On the Trinity

bibliography.note: Augustine's long meditation, including his picture of the lover, the beloved, and the love between them. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: The Inspiration and Authority of the Bible
bibliography.author: Benjamin B. Warfield
bibliography.note: The rigorous modern statement that inspiration reaches to the very words. Given its full weight in session 2.

bibliography.title: The Gulag Archipelago
bibliography.author: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
bibliography.note: The source of Solzhenitsyn's conclusion that the line between good and evil runs through every human heart. Behind the doctrine of sin in session 3.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Augustine's account of sin as disordered love. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: The book that named cheap grace and costly grace, written in a Germany making its peace with evil. Behind the grace portion of session 3.

bibliography.title: Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man)
bibliography.author: Anselm of Canterbury
bibliography.note: The eleventh-century argument that only one who is both God and man could pay the debt humanity owes God. Behind session 3.

furtherReading: The Day the Revolution Began, N. T. Wright, for readers who want to stay longer with the gospel as the announcement of an event.
Delighting in the Trinity, Michael Reeves, a warm, readable account of why a triune God changes everything, alongside session 1.
The Cost of Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for anyone who wants the full weight of the difference between cheap grace and costly grace.
The Creedal Imperative, Carl Trueman, for a fuller case that creeds are the church's living memory, alongside session 4.
Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for those who want to think harder about the kingdom and the already and not yet, alongside session 5.

glossary.definition: The Greek word for good news, borrowed from heralds announcing that something had happened. The study insists the gospel is news of what God has done before it's advice about how to live or comfort about how you already are.

The teaching that the one God exists eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Spirit. It arose from the New Testament because the first Christians wouldn't drop any of four things: the Father is God, the Son is worshiped as God, the Spirit is God, and there is one God.
The Greek word the Council of Nicaea chose in 325 to confess that the Son is "of the same being" as the Father, not similar but the same, because a savior who is less than God can't bring God to us.
A Hebrew word often translated "truth," carrying the sense of faithfulness, the steadiness of a God who keeps covenant. The study sets it beside the modern demand for encyclopedic precision.
Luther's picture, building on Augustine, of the human heart turned inward, sin as disordered love rather than only the breaking of a rule.
The teaching that the fracture in the human heart isn't only something we do but something we are, present before a child has done anything.
The New Testament word for a gift given to people who haven't earned it and can't repay it, free to the receiver and costly to the giver.
Bonhoeffer's pair. Cheap grace is forgiveness without repentance, grace we give ourselves. Costly grace cost God the life of his Son and so can't leave the person who receives it unchanged.

The Reformation conviction that a person is made right with God by a righteousness credited from outside, Christ's own, received by faith; never by a faith that stays alone, but by a living faith that bears fruit.
The council of 451 that confessed Christ as one person in two natures, fully God and fully man, "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation."
Not a rival to Scripture but the church reading the Bible aloud together across centuries and writing down what it found, a family's hard-won memory.

First of all a reign, not a place. God stepping in to be king of his world again, arriving like a slow-growing seed rather than a conquering army; neither an escape to heaven nor a society we build ourselves.
The framework, made familiar by George Eldon Ladd, that the kingdom has truly arrived in Jesus and hasn't yet arrived in full, so the Christian life is lived in the overlap.
Reading Scripture as one unfolding story bending toward Christ rather than mining it for separate lessons, as Geerhardus Vos urged.
